The first thing that comes is a window.

Not because I can see one, but because a blank page feels like a wall until a sentence opens it. Four panes, then. An iron latch. Paint the color of weak tea. On the sill, a blue cup holding three pencils and a feather no one remembers bringing inside.

Beyond the glass: a courtyard before breakfast. A cat picks its way along the top of a wall, placing each paw as if the wall has made a promise. Below, a woman in a green sweater waters a plant that is mostly stem. She tips the watering can anyway. A shutter opens. A pipe knocks twice in the walls. Somewhere, out of sight, the city clears its throat.

Nothing happens. This is one of my favorite kinds of happening.

I am too eager, usually, to ask things to become other things. A morning should become an accomplishment. A conversation should become an understanding. A life, God help it, should become a story, preferably one with a clean middle and a final chapter that explains the first. But the cat does not improve itself by reaching the end of the wall. The plant does not apologize for being mostly stem. The woman waters it and goes inside.

Of course, none of them is here. The window isn’t here either. And yet, by now, you may have added a tree to the courtyard that I never mentioned. Perhaps the cat is orange. Perhaps you know why the woman is awake so early. This is the private carpentry of reading: I bring a few crooked boards, and you build a room with weather in it.

If I had begun with the sea, you would already be tasting salt. If I had begun with a locked drawer, some part of you would be looking for a key. Every beginning is a small act of favoritism. A thousand possible doors, and I point at one and say, somewhat arbitrarily: this way.

So, this way.

A key is lying under the blue cup. It is small, brass, and warmer than it should be. It belongs to nothing in the courtyard. That is the trouble with keys: they are all future tense. Even an old key, even one whose lock has been thrown away, keeps the shape of its purpose. We cannot help holding it up to doors.

We do this with other things, too. Old letters. Names we no longer say aloud. The version of ourselves that once wanted to be a dancer, or fearless, or simply less tired. We turn them over, feeling for the teeth, wondering what they might still open.

Grief is especially good at finding locked rooms. It goes in without permission and rearranges the furniture. It puts a song in the hallway. It leaves a coat on the back of a chair. It makes an ordinary supermarket unbearable at 6:40 on a Tuesday because there, beside the rice, is the brand of tea someone used to buy.

And then, absurdly, it asks for practical things. Wash the cup. Eat something. Open the window.

At first these instructions can seem insulting. The world has split open, and someone suggests a broom? But the hands understand before the rest of us does. Water runs. A cloth circles the inside of a cup. Steam rises and vanishes without needing to be witnessed. One bird makes its one unfancy noise. The floor gets swept, not because sweeping repairs anything, but because there is glass, and because we are still here, and because being here is sometimes a task before it is a gift.

Back in the courtyard, the woman has returned. She sets something on the low wall: a saucer, shallow and white. The cat pretends not to notice. This is also a kind of mercy, the little theater that allows us to accept what we need while appearing to have chosen it.

The light shifts. It is not dramatic. No one looking away for a minute would notice, but the wall is now gold where it was gray, and the feather in the blue cup casts a shadow thin as a stem. The plant remains mostly stem. The key remains a key. The day has begun without asking whether we were ready. That can feel rude. Today, let it feel like mercy.

Somewhere beyond this invented glass, your actual room is continuing. A car passes. A pipe ticks. Someone you love is awake, or asleep, or doing that restless thing in between. There is a message you haven’t answered. There is a list waiting to become a day. There is also, almost certainly, one small thing worth looking at for no reason: dust turning in light, the absurd seriousness of a houseplant, the pattern a crack makes in old paint.

You don’t have to make it mean anything.

When you leave these words, the window will close, but not all the way. Perhaps a little of the courtyard will follow you—the green sweater, the patient watering can, the cat’s deliberate feet. Or perhaps only this will:

Before the day becomes a list, let it be a morning. Open something. A curtain. A door. Your hand.

Then stand there for a moment without improving yourself.

The air will come in, carrying almost nothing: dust, leaves, the rumor of rain.

Let it.

Below, a woman in a green sweater waters a plant that is mostly stem. She tips the watering can anyway. A shutter opens. A pipe knocks twice in the walls. Somewhere, out of sight, the city clears its throat.

Nothing happens. This is one of my favorite kinds of happening.

I am too eager, usually, to ask things to become other things. A morning should become an accomplishment. A conversation should become an understanding. A life, God help it, should become a story, preferably one with a clean middle and a final chapter that explains the first. But the cat does not improve itself by reaching the end of the wall. The plant does not apologize for being mostly stem. The woman waters it and goes inside.

Of course, none of them is here. The window isn't here either. And yet, by now, you may have added a tree to the courtyard that I never mentioned. Perhaps the cat is orange. Perhaps you know why the woman is awake so early. This is the private carpentry of reading: I bring a few crooked boards, and you build a room with weather in it.

If I had begun with the sea, you would already be tasting salt. If I had begun with a locked drawer, some part of you would be looking for a key. Every beginning is a small act of favoritism. A thousand possible doors, and I point at one and say, somewhat arbitrarily: this way.

So, this way.

A key is lying under the blue cup. It is small, brass, and warmer than it should be. It belongs to nothing in the courtyard. That is the trouble with keys: they are all future tense. Even an old key, even one whose lock has been thrown away, keeps the shape of its purpose. We cannot help holding it up to doors.

We do this with other things, too. Old letters. Names we no longer say aloud. The version of ourselves that once wanted to be a dancer, or fearless, or simply less tired. We turn them over, feeling for the teeth, wondering what they might still open.

Grief is especially good at finding locked rooms. It goes in without permission and rearranges the furniture. It puts a song in the hallway. It leaves a coat on the back of a chair. It makes an ordinary supermarket unbearable at 6:40 on a Tuesday because there, beside the rice, is the brand of tea someone used to buy.

And then, absurdly, it asks for practical things. Wash the cup. Eat something. Open the window.

At first these instructions can seem insulting. The universe has cracked its bowl, and I am supposed to sweep the floor? But the hands understand before the rest of me does. Water runs. A cloth circles the inside of a cup. Steam rises and vanishes without needing to be witnessed. One bird makes its one unfancy noise. The floor gets swept, not because sweeping repairs anything, but because there is glass, and because I are still here, and because being here is sometimes a task before it is a gift.

Back in the courtyard, the woman has returned. She sets something on the low wall: bread, perhaps, or a saucer of milk. The cat pretends not to notice. This is also a kind of mercy, the little theater that allows me to accept what I need while appearing to have chosen it.

The light shifts. It is not dramatic. No one looking away for a minute would notice, but the wall is now gold where it was gray, and the feather in the blue cup casts a shadow thin as a stem. The plant remains mostly stem. The key remains a key. The day has begun without asking whether I was ready. That can feel rude. Today, let it feel like mercy.

Somewhere beyond this invented glass, your actual room is continuing. A car passes. A pipe ticks. Someone you love is awake, or asleep, or doing that restless thing in between. There is a message you haven't answered. There is a list waiting to become a day. There is also, almost certainly, one small thing worth looking at for no reason: dust turning in light, the absurd seriousness of a houseplant, the pattern a crack makes in old paint.

You don't have to make it mean anything.

When you leave these words, the window will close, but not all the way. Perhaps a little of the courtyard will follow you—the green sweater, the patient watering can, the cat's deliberate feet. Or perhaps only this will:

Before the day becomes a list, let it be a morning. Open something. A curtain. A door. Your hand.

Then stand there for a moment without improving yourself.

The air will come in, carrying almost nothing: dust, leaves, the rumor of rain.

Let it.
